concepts.def: Trying out a range of media, techniques and processes to discover possibilities before committing to ideas.
Testing materials such as paint, ink, print, collage or digital processes to learn their qualities and limits.
First-hand material you record yourself — observational drawings, your own photographs, objects and places.
Deliberately trying unfamiliar approaches and learning from unexpected results rather than playing safe.
Short written notes explaining what you tried, what you learned and what you plan to do next.
A curated collection of experimental work showing breadth of investigation and the journey of your ideas.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Unit AS 1: Experimental Portfolio — a core area of A-Level Art & Design.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Unit AS 1: Experimental Portfolio brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Unit AS 1: Experimental Portfolio.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The main purpose of an experimental portfolio is to:
options: Practise handwriting for annotation.
Explore media, processes and ideas with breadth and ambition.
Produce one perfect final painting.
Collect only printed images from the internet.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a primary source?
options: An observational drawing you made of a market stall.
A scan from an art book.
A famous painting found online.
A classmate's photograph reused unchanged.
Retell your whole day in detail.
Describe only the weather while you worked.
Repeat the project title on every page.
Briefly explain decisions, discoveries and next steps.

mcqs.q: Risk-taking is valued in experimental work because:
options: It avoids the need for any drawing.
It removes the need to evaluate.
Unexpected results can open new directions and show ambition.
It guarantees higher marks regardless of outcome.

mcqs.q: Is a 'failed' experiment worthless in an experimental portfolio?
options: Only research carried out in a museum.
No — documented unsuccessful experiments show learning and inform next steps.
Yes — failed work must be redone until perfect.
Yes — only successful pieces should be kept.

mcqs.q: Does more annotation always mean a better portfolio?
options: No — portfolios must contain no writing at all.
No — concise, purposeful notes linked to decisions matter more than quantity.
Yes — write as much as possible on every page.
Only research carried out in a museum.
Yes — failed work must be redone until perfect.
Any image you find, as long as you redraw it yourself.
Only research carried out in a museum.
First-hand recording: your own drawings, photographs and studies from observation.
